mcqs.question: What is the key structural difference between a CartItem and an OrderItem in this model?
options: CartItem holds a live reference to Product so it reflects current data; OrderItem is an immutable snapshot of product details taken at checkout
CartItem and OrderItem are the same class, renamed depending on order status
OrderItem is only created after a return is filed, not at checkout
CartItem stores the price and OrderItem stores only the product ID
mcqs.explanation: CartItem reflects the live catalog (price, name can still change), while OrderItem freezes those facts at the moment of purchase so the order stays meaningful even after the catalog changes. They are distinct classes with different lifecycles, OrderItem is created at checkout (not at return), and OrderItem stores the full snapshot, not just an ID.

mcqs.question: Why is it wrong for an OrderItem to store only a foreign key to Product and look up its price on demand?
options: Foreign keys are slower to query than storing duplicate data in every case
A later price change to the product would retroactively and incorrectly alter what a past order appears to have charged
Product records are deleted immediately after every sale
Databases do not allow foreign keys between Order and Product tables
mcqs.explanation: The core issue is correctness over time: an order must represent what was actually charged at purchase, and a live lookup would let future catalog changes rewrite historical facts. This isn't primarily a query-speed argument, products aren't deleted after sale, and foreign keys between these tables are perfectly valid — the design choice not to rely on one here is deliberate.

mcqs.question: What is the main trade-off between reserving inventory at add-to-cart versus only at checkout?
options: Add-to-cart reservation prevents any lockup risk entirely
Checkout-time reservation guarantees zero oversell under any circumstance
Add-to-cart reservation protects stock earlier but risks locking it up in abandoned carts; checkout-time reservation limits lockup but leaves a short window for oversell during payment
There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches
mcqs.explanation: Reserving earlier protects a browsing customer's stock longer but ties up inventory in carts that may never convert; reserving later shrinks that lockup window but shifts risk to the payment window itself. Neither option eliminates lockup or oversell risk entirely, and the two approaches are meaningfully different trade-offs, not equivalent.

mcqs.question: How should a partial return of one item from a three-item order be modeled?
options: Delete the returned OrderItem from the original Order record
Edit the Order's total directly to reflect the reduced item count
Cancel the entire Order and have the customer re-purchase the remaining items
Create a separate Return entity referencing the specific returned OrderItem, leaving the original Order and its items unchanged
mcqs.explanation: A Return is a new event layered on top of the immutable order record — it references the specific OrderItem(s) involved without deleting or editing the original order, preserving what was actually purchased as a permanent fact. Deleting the item, editing the total in place, or cancelling the whole order would all destroy or misrepresent that original record.
